content: This review aimed to minimize publication bias by including randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and consulting subject matter experts. To our knowledge, this is the first review to compare the effects of animal milk, follow-on formulas, plant-based milks, lower-fat milks, and fortified milks on health outcomes in children aged 12–23 months. The evidence presented demonstrates that follow-on formulas and fortified milks provide beneficial effects on children’s micronutrient status, hemoglobin, and ferritin levels, often comparable to or exceeding those of animal milk, depending on the specific outcome. A prior review by Vandenplas (2014) concluded that follow-on formulas improve micronutrient status (e.g., iron and vitamin D) and reduce protein intake compared to animal milk, though fortified milks were not as effective in reducing protein intake. Our findings align with this review, showing that follow-on formulas effectively reduce iron deficiency anemia and improve hemoglobin and ferritin concentrations. Similarly, Sacri (2021) found that consuming follow-on formulas in volumes between 100–500 mL per day significantly improved iron status and reduced the prevalence of iron deficiency in children. A review by Matsuyama (2016) assessed the impact of fortified milk on growth and nutrient status in children aged 6–47 months. It reported positive changes in hemoglobin levels in children consuming fortified milk. Six of the eight studies included in Matsuyama’s review were also part of our analysis. However, we excluded studies that did not compare fortified milk against animal milk or that compared two follow-on formulas. Consistent with our findings, studies by Morley (1999) and Daly (1996) concluded that fortified milk is an effective complementary nutrition source for children in need when consumed in appropriate amounts alongside a normal diet. Eichler (2012) pooled data from 13 trials on fortified milk and follow-on formulas, concluding that micronutrient-fortified milk and cereal products can effectively reduce anemia in children under three years in developing countries. However, the evidence for functional health outcomes remained inconclusive. Several studies included in Eichler’s review were also part of our analysis. In conclusion, feeding children aged 12–23 months with at least 250 mL of follow-on formula or fortified milk regularly can improve their micronutrient status (e.g., vitamin D and zinc), hemoglobin levels, and ferritin concentrations, while reducing the risk of iron deficiency anemia more effectively than animal milk. Evidence also suggests that fortified milk has a similar impact on morbidity (e.g., respiratory and diarrheal episodes) and oral health as animal milk. However, the effects of follow-on formulas and fortified milk on growth indicators (e.g., weight, height, BMI) are comparable to those of animal milk. There is limited evidence on the efficacy of plant-based milks and lower-fat milks in providing similar benefits to children aged 12–23 months. Current data do not indicate any adverse effects of these interventions on children’s health or nutrient status. However, further research is needed to assess long-term outcomes, food preferences, child development, and the effects of plant-based and lower-fat milks. Additionally, more rigorous studies are required to address the heterogeneity in findings and improve the quality of evidence in this field.
